Larkmoor Valley Water Cooperative - Annual Report 2025 (fictional document)

Message from the chair
The year 2025 tested our cooperative. A dry spring and a record heatwave in July pushed demand to levels we had not seen since the cooperative was founded in 1998. Thanks to the commitment of our staff and of our 6,240 member households, supply was never interrupted.

Network and water losses
Our network now spans 412 kilometres of pipes, of which 118 kilometres are more than fifty years old. Water losses remain our main weakness. In 2025, 23 percent of the water we treated was lost through leaks before it reached a meter, compared with 26 percent in 2024. The leak detection programme launched in March located 147 leaks, most of them on cast iron mains in the northern sector. We estimate that every point of losses avoided saves about 38,000 cubic metres a year.

Water quality
All 1,860 regulatory samples taken in 2025 met the drinking water standards, with the exception of two samples in August at the Hollin Ridge reservoir, where turbidity briefly exceeded the limit after a storm. Supply from that reservoir was suspended for nine hours as a precaution.

Finances
Revenue reached 9.4 million euros, an increase of 4 percent. Operating costs rose faster, by 11 percent, mainly because of electricity prices and chemical reagents. The cooperative therefore closes the year with a deficit of 310,000 euros, the first deficit in eight years. This deficit is covered by our reserves, which stand at 2.1 million euros at year end.

Tariff
The board of directors considers that a moderate tariff increase is unavoidable. It will propose to the general assembly an increase of 6 percent of the volumetric price from 1 April 2026, while keeping the fixed subscription unchanged so that small consumers are protected. The board rejected a larger increase that would have restored balance in a single year.

Recommendations
The board makes three recommendations to the general assembly. First, double the annual budget for pipe renewal, from 1.2 to 2.4 million euros, starting in 2026. Second, install smart meters in the 900 households of the northern sector to detect leaks on private connections. Third, sign a long-term electricity supply contract to reduce exposure to market prices.

Outlook
We expect losses to fall below 20 percent by 2028 if the renewal programme is funded. Climate projections for the valley suggest that dry summers will become more frequent, and the cooperative must prepare for them now.
